meta.title: An investigation of mental imagery in bipolar disorder: Exploring "the mind's eye"
meta.domain: Clinical psychology / psychiatry — mental imagery in bipolar disorder and mood instability
meta.overview: Cross-sectional case-control study (N=131) giving people with bipolar disorder, unipolar depression, anxiety disorders, and non-clinical controls a battery of subjective imagery, emotional-imagery, and cognitive imagery tasks. Bipolar disorder is marked by heightened impact of intrusive prospective (emotional) imagery, but basic cognitive imagery stages are intact and the emotional-imagery abnormality is transdiagnostic (tracks affective lability rather than diagnosis).
meta.abstract: People with bipolar disorder (BD) reported greater impact of intrusive prospective mental imagery in daily life than non-clinical controls, while showing no clear abnormalities in the basic cognitive stages of imagery (generation, inspection, manipulation) and even superior visual short-term memory. When matched for depression and anxiety, these emotional-imagery abnormalities were not specific to BD, suggesting emotional mental imagery is a transdiagnostic marker of affective lability rather than a BD-specific deficit.

claims.statement: Bipolar disorder is associated with greater daily-life impact of intrusive prospective mental imagery than non-clinical controls (IFES 29.87 vs 17.42, p<0.001).
Basic cognitive stages of mental imagery (generation, inspection, manipulation) are largely intact in bipolar disorder.
Emotional-imagery abnormalities are not specific to bipolar disorder when matched for depression and anxiety — a transdiagnostic marker.
People with bipolar disorder show superior visual short-term memory recall vs controls (0.65 vs 0.53, p=0.04).
Across all groups, higher affective lability is associated with greater impact of emotional prospective imagery (beta=0.293, p=.001).

contributions.typing_rationale: First comprehensive evaluation combining cognitive and emotional/subjective imagery domains in bipolar disorder within one sample.
Shows basic (non-emotional) imagery processes are preserved in BD, supporting the feasibility of imagery-based therapies.
Frames emotional mental imagery as a transdiagnostic marker of affective lability rather than a BD-specific abnormality, consistent with the 'emotional amplifier' hypothesis.

sota.resolver_notes: Undermind semantic search (year_max=2016) confirmed a dense, well-cited prior neighborhood largely from the same Holmes group: Holmes 2011 (emotional imagery and mood instability), Holmes 2008 (imagery as emotional amplifier — the founding hypothesis), Ivins 2014 (imagery in bipolar vs unipolar), and Gregory 2010 (intrusive imagery in bipolar). This paper is the comprehensive extension of that program, so finding-level overlap is high (moderate novelty relative to a mature line).
